title: Through the Roof
lead: The faith of friends opens a way where the sick man could never get on his own.
questions: Whom could you carry to Jesus this week, even by one corner of the mat, and what is your piece of roof to tear open?
Who once carried you when your faith was barely breathing, and have you ever told them?
Where in your church, or in which of your habits, are you standing like the crowd in the doorway, making it harder for someone to reach Jesus?
note: Scripture quotations are from the Berean Standard Bible (public domain) unless otherwise noted.

paragraphs: We know almost nothing about the main character of this story: we don’t know his name or how long he had been paralyzed. But we do know something that will turn out to matter most: he had four people close to him. Mark doesn’t call them friends, though the way they act shows remarkable care for the sick man. Jesus is teaching in a house in Capernaum, where so many people gather that “there was no more room, not even outside the door.” Inside, in the best seats, sit the teachers of the Law; around them stands a crowd of the healthy and the devout; and behind that wall of backs, a stretcher stops, carrying a man who cannot walk. No one moves aside. A house full of people listening to the Word has become an obstacle for the one who needed Christ most urgently. It is possible to crowd so tightly around Jesus that the sick cannot reach Him.

So the four decide to go over the top: they climb the outside stairs onto a roof of beams, reed mats and packed earth, which could be taken apart by hand fairly quickly and repaired the same day. Their faith was not a mood. It was physical labor and the risk of a scene. When the mat comes down through the hole in the ceiling, Mark writes: “When Jesus saw their faith.” Theirs, not his. There are times when a person “hangs” entirely on someone else’s faith, and that faith counts with God too. Jesus’ first words surprise everyone: He doesn’t say “Get up,” but “your sins are forgiven.” He said those words to no one else He healed; perhaps this one man needed exactly those words first. Jesus heals in the order of needs, not of symptoms.

The scholars think: blasphemy, because only God forgives sins, and only through a sacrifice, a priest, a temple. Here there is only an ordinary house and nothing but a word. Either this is a crime, or something unheard of is happening. They are right about the alternative, but they choose the wrong option. So Jesus does the harder thing, the thing that can be checked, “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins”: the man gets up, picks up his mat and walks out through a crowd that now knows how to make way. Mark will bracket his whole book with the theme of blasphemy: it is at the center of the first dispute, in Capernaum, and of the last one, before the high priest, which ends in a death sentence. For what He said over that stretcher, He will pay the highest price.

Every role in this scene is up for grabs: the crowd that blocks the way; the experts who evaluate and ask for nothing; and the four without whom there would be no story at all. Think about which of them you are, and look around to see whose stretcher is waiting outside your house of prayer.

The section we close today is addressed to the waiting, the defeated, the avoided and the immobilized. We have already met Simeon and Anna, who waited their whole lives; Simon, defeated over his empty nets; and the woman from Sychar whom everyone avoided. One addressee remains: a man who can’t get anywhere on his own. We know almost nothing about the main character of today’s story: we don’t know his name, his age, or how long he had been paralyzed. What will turn out to matter most is what we do know: four people carried him. Mark doesn’t call them friends, though the way they act shows that the sick man meant a great deal to them.

sections.heading: A House No One Could Get Into
paragraphs: Jesus returns to Capernaum, His base by the lake. It was not a large village; archaeologists have measured it along the shore and estimated that no more than about fifteen hundred people lived there, in houses of dark basalt clustered around shared courtyards. News that He “was home” gets around a small place like that in fifteen minutes. Mark describes the result: people gather in such numbers “that there was no more room, not even outside the door.” At this point the quiet drama of this scene begins. Inside there are also teachers of the Law; they came early and took the best seats, close to Jesus. Around them stands a crowd of the healthy, the curious, the devout. Outside, behind that wall of backs, a stretcher stops, carrying a man who cannot walk. No one moves aside. A house full of people listening to the Word has become an impassable obstacle for the one who needed Christ most urgently. It is a picture every community should pause over: it is possible to crowd so tightly around Jesus that the sick cannot reach Him. Closeness can become a form of blockade.

sections.heading: The Four
paragraphs: Then the four people carrying the sick man make a decision that sets this story apart: if they can’t get in through the door, they will go over the top. They climb the outside stairs to the roof and start taking it apart. That sounds like vandalism, until you picture a roof of that time: beams, reed mats laid across them, and a layer of packed earth on top. The roof was also an ordinary living space, not an untouchable covering: people went up by ladder or stairs, slept there on hot nights, dried their stores, and in tightly built villages a family on a higher terrace treated the roof of the neighbor below as an extension of its own yard. A ceiling like that could be taken apart by hand fairly quickly and repaired the same day; the narrow basalt walls of Capernaum’s houses couldn’t have carried anything heavier anyway. This was determination, not an act of vandalism. The fact remains, though, that they were digging through someone else’s roof in front of the whole village, over the heads of distinguished guests, risking a scene and a bill for the repairs. The faith of these four was not a mood but physical labor: lifting, climbing, digging through packed clay, taking responsibility for the damage. When the mat with the sick man comes down through the hole in the ceiling, Mark writes the sentence at the heart of this story: “When Jesus saw their faith.” Theirs, not his. About the sick man’s own faith the text is silent; we don’t know what he was thinking. What we can be sure of is that Jesus saw the trust in the hearts of the people who brought him. Carrying someone’s stretcher is one of the oldest ministries of the church, older than all its offices.

sections.heading: “Son, Your Sins Are Forgiven”
paragraphs: Jesus’ first words surprise everyone, the sick man included. He doesn’t say “Get up,” but: “Son, your sins are forgiven.” A tender form of address, “Son,” and release from guilt for a man who wanted healthy legs. In the biblical account there is no other healing scene in which Jesus says these words; only this man heard them before he was healed. It isn’t stated outright, but perhaps that is exactly what he needed. Elsewhere in Scripture Jesus clearly rejects the simple scheme in which every illness is a punishment for personal sin. There is a lesson in discernment here that everyone who helps others needs: a person’s real need is not always the one they were brought in with. Sometimes under legs that don’t work lies a restless conscience, and sometimes under a pious question lies loneliness. Jesus heals in the order of needs, not in the order of symptoms.

sections.heading: “He Is Blaspheming!”
paragraphs: The teachers of the Law who see this react in their thoughts, and Mark wrote those thoughts down: “Who can forgive sins but God alone?” We have to do them justice: they are right. Blasphemy in the strict sense means reaching for what belongs to God alone, and forgiving sins is one of those prerogatives. What’s more, forgiveness had its appointed path: a sacrifice, a priest, the temple. And here is some teacher from Nazareth, in an ordinary house, with no altar, no blood and no priest, declaring a man’s sins forgiven by His word alone, on His own authority. Either something unheard of is happening, or this is the gravest crime there is. The scholars see the alternative correctly; their only mistake is assuming it is the latter. The title Jesus uses in this scene is also worth noticing: the Son of Man. In the Gospels it is used almost exclusively by Jesus Himself, when He speaks about Himself. It is a title ambiguous enough not to give His opponents grounds for a charge, while reminding attentive listeners of the figure in Daniel’s prophecy to whom authority is given. Jesus doesn’t make quick classification easy for anyone. He leaves the question open long enough that each person has to answer it personally. In fact, Mark built a frame around his entire book with this word. Jesus’ first dispute with the scholars begins with the charge of blasphemy and the title Son of Man, and the last trial before the high priest will end with a verdict of blasphemy, and the same title will stand in the background. What He said over this stretcher would one day become the pretext for sending Him to the cross. The forgiveness that was given freely in Capernaum was not cheap.

sections.heading: Which Is Easier?
paragraphs: Jesus doesn’t leave the dispute hanging. He asks a question: “Which is easier: to say to a paralytic, ‘Your sins are forgiven,’ or to say, ‘Get up, pick up your mat, and walk’?” Of course the first is easier to say: forgiveness can’t be seen, and no one can check a declaration. The second sentence verifies itself within three seconds. That is exactly why Jesus does the harder thing, the one that can be checked, “so that you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins.” The healing of the legs is evidence in an invisible matter: if His word raises a paralyzed man, you can trust the same word when it says “forgiven.” The man gets up, picks up his mat and walks out in front of everyone, through the crowd that an hour earlier couldn’t make way for him. Now it lets him through. Mark records the reaction: amazement and praise, “We have never seen anything like this!” Indeed they hadn’t: forgiveness had just walked through the middle of the village on its own two feet.

sections.heading: Whose Faith Carries
paragraphs: Let’s go over the cast of this scene once more, because it is a mirror for every community. There is the sick man, who can’t get there on his own. There is the crowd of the devout, who blocked the entrance. There are the scholars in the best seats, who came to evaluate and even think correctly, just fruitlessly: of everyone in the scene, they alone received nothing, because they asked for nothing. And there are the four, who don’t have a single line to speak in this story, but without whom there would be no story at all. The gospel didn’t record their names, only their faith, the only faith Jesus “saw” in this scene. It’s worth asking yourself a simple question: who am I in this scene? Because every one of these roles is up for grabs in every community, every week. You can be the crowd that blocks access by sheer mass. You can be the expert who evaluates everything correctly and helps nobody. Or one of the four: on the stretcher, on the stairs, tearing open the roof, praying for someone who no longer prays for themselves.

sections.heading: For Today
paragraphs: If you are the one lying on the stretcher today, immobilized by illness, depression, age or a situation with no way out, this story tells you two things. First: your carriers count. The faith of the people who carry you, pray for you and look for a hole in the roof on your behalf is seen by Jesus and works in your favor, even when your own faith is barely breathing. Second: Christ sees under your paralysis what others don’t see, and He starts with the deepest need, not the most visible one. If, however, you are among the healthy today, pay attention to where you are standing. Check that you’re not standing right in the doorway. And look around to see whose stretcher is waiting outside your house of prayer, because it is almost certainly waiting somewhere. The four men from Capernaum had no theology to offer; they had only the four corners of a mat and sheer stubbornness. It turned out that was exactly enough for a man to meet God.
